answers.answer:
Two retail pea powders bought online and in Cork, Ireland, in 2016 and 2017 contained 40.6 and 15.4 µg/kg cadmium and 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg lead, as sold.

What heavy metals have been measured in pea protein? Retail pea powders from Ireland were measured for lead, cadmium, total mercury, total chromium, and tin, and not for arsenic. Cadmium in the two pea packages was 40.6 and 15.4 µg/kg, and lead was 22.2 and 22.5 µg/kg, as sold. Pea concentrates from an online market were measured for nickel, total chromium, cadmium, and lead, and not for arsenic or mercury. Nickel means were 585.49 and 268.27 µg/kg and total chromium means were 78.97 and 114.11 µg/kg, with cadmium and lead not detected. A non-detect is not a measured zero when the detection limit's unit is not restated, which is the case for those concentrate footnotes.

How do cadmium and lead get into peas? The plant takes cadmium and lead up from soil, and contaminated dust or waste can add more, which is why site matters. Soil pH, the variety, and the fertilizer program change uptake, according to a review of dietary cadmium by FDA scientists. In South Cairo and Giza, pea fruit beside cement, iron, brick, and fertilizer works held 1,025 mg/kg cadmium and 121 mg/kg lead, dry weight. Fruit from the study's other farms held 2.6 mg/kg cadmium and 8.9 mg/kg lead, dry weight, which is lower than the polluted fruit and still high next to retail powders. Those fruit results explain the crop pathway, and they are not the concentration of a protein isolate.

Does making an isolate concentrate the metals? Protein separation discards starch and fiber and dries the protein fraction, so a metal that follows the protein can be higher per kilogram in the powder than in the seed. No paper in this set measured the same lot as seed and as isolate, so that concentration is not a measured factor here. European law sets cadmium at 40 µg/kg for pulses and at 100 µg/kg for proteins from pulses, which leaves room for a more concentrated ingredient. The Irish pea powders at 15.4 and 40.6 µg/kg cadmium are under the protein row, and two packages do not show how often that happens. Heat does not destroy the elements, so a roasting step is not, by itself, a removal step.

Are Canadian, Chinese, or European peas lower? None of the powder studies records the country where the peas were grown, so Canada, China, and the European Union cannot be ranked as isolate origins. The Irish powders were bought in Ireland, and the concentrates were bought online for a laboratory in Spain. A Canadian Grain Commission paper on field pea seed reports a mean cadmium of 0.023 mg/kg in its abstract, with arsenic and lead below 0.050 mg/kg. The full article is closed, the sample table was not read, and the material is whole seed rather than isolate. A sourcing preference needs origin on the lot, the same form, and the same basis, and those three are not together in this library.

How do pea powders compare with whey and other plant powders? In the Irish survey the two pea powders were higher in cadmium than most of the 27 whey powders and lower than the two mixed plant powders. Whey cadmium ran from below 0.61 to 23.2 µg/kg, pea was 15.4 and 40.6, and mixed plant was 45.1 and 58.1. Lead did not follow cadmium: pea was about 22 µg/kg and the highest lead result was 88.4 µg/kg in a whey powder. Among two pea and two rice concentrates, detected lead was in one rice product, and total chromium was higher in both rice products than in either pea product. Two or four products are a comparison inside one study, not a ranking of the world's pea protein against the world's whey.

What legal limits apply? Proteins from pulses have a European cadmium maximum of 0.10 mg/kg, and other pulses have 0.040 mg/kg. Those rows were set in the 2021 cadmium amendment and are carried in the contaminants regulation now in force. Food supplements have a cadmium maximum of 1.0 mg/kg as placed on the market, except the higher seaweed and bivalve supplement row. Nickel in pulses except dry beans and lupins is 4.0 mg/kg from 1 July 2025, and that row is not written as proteins from pulses. A processed food that is not a listed category uses the regulation's concentration rules rather than a blank cell or an invented number.

What should a laboratory report include? The report should name the form, such as isolate, concentrate, or blend, and the basis, such as as sold or dry weight. It should list lead, cadmium, total arsenic, inorganic arsenic if rice is in the product, total mercury, and nickel, each with its own result. The quantification limit should sit well below the maximum that applies, for example well below 100 µg/kg where the protein cadmium row applies. The method should be an acid digestion and a mass-spectrometric or equivalent determination, with the lot identity on the same page. A non-detect should show the limit, and a limit whose unit is not stated cannot be used as a food concentration.

Do the concentrate non-detects mean the cadmium is very low? The paper marks cadmium and lead as not detected in both pea concentrates. The footnotes give limits below 0.015 and below 0.026 and do not restate whether that unit is the digest or the food. A food limit of quantification near 0.02 µg/kg would be unusually low next to the Irish method, which reported cadmium down to below 0.61 µg/kg in a whey powder. Until the unit is clear, the honest statement is that the concentrates did not report a detected cadmium or lead value. It is not a finding that those products sit at a fraction of a microgram per kilogram.

Was arsenic measured? Arsenic was not among the elements in the Irish protein-powder method. The concentrate mineral table that includes nickel, chromium, cadmium, and lead does not include arsenic or mercury. Garden pea fruit in Egypt was measured for total arsenic, at 0.03 mg/kg on unpolluted-site fruit and 0.1 mg/kg on polluted-site fruit, dry weight, without speciation. Boiled frozen peas in the US Total Diet Study were not detected for total arsenic at a reporting limit of 3 µg/kg, which is the vegetable and not the powder. If a product also contains rice, inorganic arsenic has to be asked for separately, because these pea-only tables do not supply it.

Should the Egyptian pea results change how powders are read? They should change how the crop is understood, and they should not be pasted onto a protein specification. The polluted fruit is evidence that industrial waste near the field can push pea cadmium and lead into the hundreds or thousands of milligrams per kilogram, dry weight. The unpolluted fruit in the same provinces was already 2.6 mg/kg cadmium, dry weight, which is not what the Irish retail powders showed. The table keeps that fruit as its own form so the powder rows stay readable beside it. A buyer of isolate should ask where the crop was grown and for a lot result, and should not treat either Egyptian mean as the expected powder concentration.

How do frozen peas compare? The US Total Diet Study measured frozen green peas after boiling, as the food is eaten. Three composites showed cadmium in two, up to 3.2 µg/kg, with a reporting limit of 1 µg/kg. Lead, total mercury, and total arsenic were not detected, at reporting limits of 4, 1, and 3 µg/kg. Those figures are as consumed and water-rich, so they sit far below a dry protein on a per-kilogram basis for reasons of water as well as process. They belong on the frozen pea record as the vegetable, and they are cited here only to keep the powder from being confused with the vegetable.

What is still too thin to settle? Two retail packages and two concentrates do not make a distribution, a percentile, or a pass rate for the ingredient. Growing origin is missing on the powders, and the Canadian seed baseline is an abstract without its table. Inorganic arsenic and, for the concentrates, mercury were not measured. No before-and-after process trial shows how much metal the isolate step keeps. Those gaps are why the page states what was measured and does not offer a regional winner or a removal percentage.
